title: Dusasa II
medium: Found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks
altText: A very large, wall-sized hanging artwork made of many small pieces of metal and plastic joined with wire, so that it ripples and folds like a shimmering cloth. The surface is a patchwork of repeated pieces, and the shape can fall in soft folds.

context: El Anatsui is a Ghanaian artist, born in Anyako in 1944. This 2007 work is made from found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks, and measures 236 by 288 inches, roughly 6 by 7.3 meters. It is large enough to cover an entire wall.

descriptions.k: This giant artwork is made of tiny pieces of metal, joined together with wire. It hangs like a huge shiny cloth. Can you imagine how many pieces there are? Where would you hang it?
descriptions.g12: El Anatsui is an artist from Ghana in Africa. He made this giant artwork from found metal pieces joined with wire. It hangs on a wall like a shimmering cloth. It is about as tall as a two-story house! Why do you think he used leftover materials?
descriptions.g35: El Anatsui, an artist from Ghana, made Dusasa II in 2007 from found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks. It measures about 6 by 7.3 meters, big enough to cover a whole wall. Thousands of small pieces are joined into something that hangs and folds like cloth. How does an artist turn leftover materials into something shimmering and beautiful?
descriptions.g68: El Anatsui, born in Ghana in 1944, made Dusasa II in 2007 from found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks. At 236 by 288 inches, it is a vast, wall-sized sculpture that hangs and folds like fabric rather than standing like a statue. The Met tags it as Abstraction. Notice how small, repeated pieces join to form a larger pattern, and how that makes you think about cloth, recycling, and the many hands behind a single work.
descriptions.g910: Dusasa II (2007) is a monumental hanging work by Ghanaian artist El Anatsui, made from found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks. It measures about 6 by 7.3 meters, yet it behaves like a textile, with folds that can change from one installation to another. By assembling many small, discarded materials into one shimmering field, Anatsui blurs lines between sculpture, painting, and cloth. Viewers can consider how scale, repetition, and reuse turn the ordinary into something grand.
descriptions.g1112: El Anatsui's Dusasa II (2007) transforms found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks into a monumental, textile-like wall sculpture of some 6 by 7.3 meters. Its flexibility resists the fixed identity usually expected of sculpture, and its repeated, joined units suggest both a collective labor and a reworking of discarded materials. The Met tags it as Abstraction, but readings that connect it to cloth traditions, global trade, consumption, or memory are also available, and the record does not settle among them.

teacherNote.context: Made in 2007 by Ghanaian artist El Anatsui from found aluminum, copper wire, and plastic disks. It measures 236 by 288 inches. Check the image before classroom use, since only metadata was read.
directions: Have students collect clean recycled materials and join them into a patterned surface, then discuss how the pieces change when joined.
Ask students to compare the work with a cloth pattern from their own community and talk about how both are built from small repeated units.
Discuss what happens to the meaning of an object when it is reused in an artwork.
